title: State Efforts to Restrict Voter-Driven Marijuana Reforms (2023–2025). So Whom Do Our Representatives Really Represent?

content_html_sanitized:
There is a cliche in journalism, “The Big Story”, but sometimes the story really is almost too big, especially if we don’t see the many small parts.

Recently, I realized that there have been a number of attempts by our lords and masters, otherwise known as our elected representatives, to stop the public’s efforts to reform various state and local marijuana laws. 

So, being old and lazy, I decided to ask my close personal friend, ChatGPT, to look into it and give me a report. Ten minutes later, this was the result. I did write the headline, and I will repeat: Whom do our elected representatives really represent?

From ChatGPT:

Over the past two years, several U.S. states have pursued measures to limit or obstruct voter-led marijuana law reforms. These actions – by legislatures, courts, and executive officials – have targeted the ballot initiative and referendum process that voters have used to enact medical cannabis legalization, recreational use laws, and decriminalization policies. Below is a summary of key state-by-state efforts, including proposed restrictions on direct democracy, their motivations, and the impact on marijuana-related ballot measures.

Legislative Attempts to Curb Marijuana Ballot Measures

  • Ohio: In 2023, Ohio’s Republican-led legislature placed Issue 1 on a special August ballot to raise the threshold for approving future constitutional amendments from a simple majority to 60%. This was widely seen as a preemptive move to make it harder for voters to pass initiatives on issues like abortion and marijuana legalization . (Ohio had a marijuana legalization measure pending for November 2023.) Voters defeated Issue 1 in August 2023, preserving the 50% threshold. Consequently, Ohioans were able to approve a recreational marijuana initiative in November 2023 with ~57% support, a measure that would have failed under the higher threshold . After that voter win, however, Ohio lawmakers moved in early 2025 to roll back parts of the voter-approved law – for example, a Senate bill was introduced to halve the home-grow limit and impose THC potency caps, steering the program away from what voters authorized . This reflects ongoing tension between the legislature and the electorate’s pro-cannabis vote.

    Idaho: Idaho has taken one of the most direct steps to bar voter-driven cannabis reform. In March 2025, the legislature approved House Joint Resolution 4 (HJR 4) to amend the state constitution and reserve all decisions on marijuana (and other controlled substances) to the legislature . If approved by voters in the November 2026 election, this amendment would prevent any future citizen initiatives from legalizing or decriminalizing cannabis by banning such measures from the ballot . The push for HJR 4 came as activists in Idaho began collecting signatures for a 2026 adult-use legalization initiative, meaning Idahoans could paradoxically face two conflicting questions in 2026: whether to legalize cannabis and whether to strip themselves of the power to legalize it . Idaho lawmakers backing HJR 4 argue that decisions on drugs should rest with elected officials; the state’s general stance remains very anti-cannabis (Idaho is one of only a handful of states with no medical marijuana, and in 2025 it even imposed new fines for small-scale possession) .

    Missouri: Following Missouri voters’ approval of a 2022 constitutional amendment legalizing recreational marijuana, the GOP-dominated legislature has sought to make citizen-initiated amendments harder to enact. In 2023 and 2024, lawmakers debated various proposals to raise the bar for initiatives – such as increasing petition signature requirements and adding supermajority or turnout-based hurdles . One 2025 proposal would require initiative campaigns to gather signatures from 15% of voters in all congressional districts (up from the current 8% in two-thirds of districts) and would mandate that a ballot measure not only win a simple majority, but also that the “Yes” votes equal at least 35% of all ballots cast in that election . Voting-rights advocates warn this would create an “impossible threshold” in low-turnout votes . Republican sponsors openly admit they believe the initiative process is being “hijacked” by progressive causes at odds with the legislature’s preferences. 

  • Marijuana reform falls into that category – it passed with 53% voter approval in Missouri, despite opposition from many state lawmakers. These efforts have not yet been enacted as of 2025 (any changes would themselves require voter approval), but they underscore the political motive: preventing voters from easily enacting policies like cannabis reform that the legislature would not pass .

    North Dakota: North Dakota’s legislature has repeatedly tried to restrain direct democracy after voters showed willingness to consider measures outside lawmakers’ control (voters legalized medical marijuana in 2016, and although a 2022 recreational cannabis initiative failed at the polls, other voter initiatives – e.g. term limits in 2022 – have passed). In 2023, legislators passed a measure to raise the signature requirement for citizen-initiated constitutional amendments from 4% to 5% of the state’s population . While 5% may sound small, North Dakota uniquely bases the requirement on total resident population rather than number of voters, making its petition bar one of the highest in practice . (At 4%, campaigns already needed ~31,000 signatures; by contrast, 4% of the last gubernatorial vote would be only ~13,600 .) This change was set for voter approval on the 2024 ballot . Earlier, in 2021, the legislature even referred a constitutional amendment to require that any voter-approved amendment appear on the ballot twice (in two successive elections) to take effect – a burdensome repeat-vote requirement similar to Nevada’s process. North Dakota voters defeated that proposal when it came to a vote (they rejected the “pass twice” requirement in the 2022 election) . These moves were broadly motivated by legislators’ frustration with citizen initiatives (one legislator called the process “a way to bypass us”). Although not aimed at any single issue, had the two-election rule been in place earlier, it could have thwarted the 2016 medical marijuana initiative (which passed once) or any future recreational marijuana measures.

    Arkansas: In Arkansas, the clash has come both at the ballot box and in court. The Republican legislature referred a measure in 2022 that would have required a 60% supermajority for future constitutional amendments and citizen laws – an effort widely seen as a response to recent voter initiatives on marijuana and other issues. Arkansas voters rejected that change in November 2022 , preserving a simple majority rule. Nonetheless, state officials have found other ways to constrain marijuana initiatives. For the 2024 election, activists proposed “Issue 3,” a ballot measure to expand the state’s medical marijuana program (including allowing home cultivation and additional qualifying conditions) . Crucially, Issue 3 also contained a clause that would legalize adult-use cannabis in Arkansas if federal law ever changed to allow it. The measure’s title, however, framed it purely as a medical marijuana expansion. In a pre-election challenge, the Arkansas Supreme Court ruled the ballot title misleading – because voters might not realize a “Yes” vote could one day trigger full legalization – and ordered that votes on Issue 3 not be counted . This effectively nullified the effort despite the issue appearing on the ballot. (It followed a similar saga in 2022, when Arkansas’s Board of Election Commissioners attempted to block a recreational marijuana initiative over its ballot summary; the state Supreme Court let that 2022 measure proceed to a vote , though ultimately a majority of voters rejected recreational legalization that year.) The Arkansas officials’ justification has centered on technical compliance with ballot laws (arguing voters must not be misled), but advocates see a pattern of using stringent title requirements and legal technicalities to keep popular cannabis measures from succeeding.

    Mississippi: Mississippi stands out in that voters currently have no avenue to change marijuana laws at the ballot. The state’s citizen initiative process was suspended after a May 2021 Mississippi Supreme Court decision that struck down a voter-approved medical marijuana initiative on procedural grounds. The court not only invalidated the medical cannabis measure but also declared the entire initiative mechanism “unworkable” (due to a constitutional quirk in how congressional districts were referenced) . This left Mississippi without any citizen-driven ballot process. In 2022, the legislature did respond by enacting a medical marijuana program via statute, but recreational marijuana remains illegal – and voters are effectively barred from initiating any legalization or decriminalization reforms themselves unless the legislature reinstates the ballot amendment process. Throughout 2023 and into 2024, Mississippi lawmakers discussed restoring an initiative process, but disagreements (e.g. over signature thresholds and legislative control) stalled those efforts. Thus, through inaction, Mississippi’s government has blocked direct democracy on cannabis (and all issues), thwarting what had been a clear voter mandate for reform.


  • Judicial and Executive Actions Targeting Marijuana Initiatives

  • Florida: In Florida, where a constitutional amendment requires a 60% supermajority to pass, marijuana advocates have worked to get adult-use legalization on the 2024 ballot. State officials – notably Attorney General Ashley Moody – attempted to derail this effort in court. After activists gathered over 1 million valid signatures for the initiative, AG Moody filed briefs urging the Florida Supreme Court to reject the measure . She argued the ballot summary was misleading – in part because it did not spell out that marijuana remains illegal federally . Moody also claimed the initiative violated Florida’s single-subject rule by both decriminalizing cannabis use and authorizing its sale . In April 2024, the Florida Supreme Court unanimously disagreed and allowed the initiative to proceed, finding its provisions “logically related” under a dominant plan of legalization . (The Court noted the summary even acknowledged it wouldn’t change federal law, undercutting Moody’s argument of voter deception .) With the legal hurdle cleared, the recreational marijuana amendment (now Amendment 3 (2024)) went before voters – but fell short of the 60% requirement, garnering ~56% approval . Thus, Florida’s existing rules (the supermajority threshold) ultimately blocked the reform despite majority support . It’s a case where both the judicial review process and a high vote threshold serve as gatekeepers. Past initiatives in Florida (including a 2016 medical marijuana measure) have also faced intense pre-ballot court scrutiny, and in 2021 the state’s high court struck down a different recreational cannabis proposal for unclear wording. These patterns show Florida officials actively policing initiatives – often citing legal technicalities – which reform advocates contend is done to shield politically unpopular opinions (like Tallahassee’s anti-cannabis stance) from being overturned by voters.

  • South Dakota: South Dakota voters approved a constitutional amendment to legalize recreational marijuana in November 2020, but they never got to see it take effect. Republican Governor Kristi Noem’s administration instigated a lawsuit to invalidate the voter-approved amendment almost immediately after the election . In 2021, the South Dakota Supreme Court upheld a lower court’s ruling that nullified the amendment on procedural grounds . The court agreed that the measure violated the state’s single-subject rule for ballot questions (the amendment covered cannabis for adults, medical marijuana, and hemp in one package) and therefore could not stand . This high-profile case – Thom v. Barnett – overturned the will of 54% of voters. Gov. Noem, who had called marijuana a “social ill,” openly celebrated the decision as a win . The episode reveals how a state’s executive branch and judiciary can combine to block voter-driven marijuana reform. Advocates did manage to put a simpler recreational statutory initiative (Initiated Measure 27) on the South Dakota ballot in 2022, but that one narrowly failed at the polls (approximately 47% in favor). The 2021 court invalidation dampened momentum and sowed confusion, illustrating the chilling effect such judicial interventions can have. South Dakota’s legislature has also attempted to raise the hurdles for ballot measures in general – for example, referring a 2022 question (Amendment C) that would have required 60% approval for any initiative affecting taxes or spending, which voters rejected . Taken together, South Dakota’s elected leaders have sent a consistent message of resistance to voter-led cannabis reform, using legal technicalities to overturn results or pushing for higher thresholds to prevent future measures.

  • Nebraska: Nebraska is a state where voters signaled strong support for marijuana reform only to face ongoing legal battles fueled by elected officials and former officials. In November 2024, Nebraskans overwhelmingly approved two medical marijuana initiatives – one to legalize medicinal cannabis and one to establish a regulatory commission – with roughly 67%–71% of the vote . However, those initiatives were allowed on the ballot only provisionally due to a pre-election lawsuit by a former state senator, John Kuehn . Kuehn alleged that thousands of petition signatures were fraudulent or invalid. A state trial court rejected his claims and allowed the measures to be counted and certified . Undeterred, Kuehn (an outspoken marijuana opponent) filed new litigation after the election, now arguing that any state marijuana legalization is unconstitutional because it conflicts with the federal Controlled Substances Act . This novel federal-preemption argument effectively seeks to void the voter-approved laws on supremacy clause grounds – despite many other states having legal cannabis regimes coexisting with federal law. As of early 2025, the case is pending and the Nebraska Supreme Court may ultimately decide if the initiatives stand . Nebraska’s top elected Republicans have sided with the challenge: the state Attorney General and a U.S. senator (Nebraska’s former governor) penned an op-ed urging the legislature not to implement the medical cannabis program until the courts rule, calling the voter mandate “shaky” due to the alleged petition fraud and legal uncertainties . In short, even landslide voter approval has not protected Nebraska’s marijuana reforms from being stymied – opponents quickly moved the fight to the courts, raising procedural and constitutional objections to override the electorate.

    Texas (Local Initiatives): Texas does not allow statewide ballot initiatives, but several of its cities have used local referendums to advance marijuana reform – prompting a forceful pushback from state officials. In 2022, voters in multiple Texas cities (including Austin, San Marcos, Denton, Killeen, and others) approved citywide ballot measures to decriminalize misdemeanor marijuana possession, barring local police from enforcing low-level pot offenses. These wins for reform were met with immediate resistance. Some city councils attempted to overturn or ignore the voter directives (for example, the Harker Heights city council repealed a decrim ordinance before a backlash forced a new vote). At the state level, Governor Greg Abbott and Republican legislators criticized the local measures, insisting that municipalities cannot “override” state drug laws . In 2023, Texas’s legislature and Attorney General took steps to preempt these local cannabis policies. A sweeping law (HB 2127, dubbed the “Death Star” bill) was enacted to strip cities of authority to enact ordinances in broad policy areas – likely invalidating local drug decriminalization among many other local regulations (this law took effect September 2023 amidst multiple lawsuits). Then in early 2025, the Texas Senate advanced a more explicit bill to ban local marijuana initiatives outright . The proposal, responding to the wave of city reforms, would prohibit any city or county from placing on the ballot an initiative that stops enforcement of state drug laws . It even threatens city governments with hefty fines ($25,000 for a first offense) for attempting such measures . Texas’s Attorney General has also sued cities (like San Marcos) to block implementation of voter-approved decriminalization, and a state appeals court recently sided with the state, ruling San Marcos’s cannabis non-enforcement policy improper . This tug-of-war in Texas highlights an executive and legislative strategy to preempt local voter drug reforms, driven by the argument that state law must be uniformly enforced. The impact is chilling: even as activists continue to organize city cannabis initiatives, the state’s interventions have stalled several ordinances and could deter future local votes. Texas officials have made clear that, in their view, local democracy cannot be allowed to liberalize marijuana policy where state leaders refuse to do so.

  • Motivations and Impact

These state-by-state battles reveal a common theme: many restrictions on ballot measures emerged only after voters began approving policies – like marijuana legalization – that state lawmakers opposed. Officials often justify the new barriers in procedural terms (ensuring “accurate” ballot language, preventing out-of-state influence, protecting the constitution from hasty changes, etc.), but critics note that the timing correlates with voter-endorsed marijuana reforms. In Missouri, for example, one supporter of stricter initiative rules argued the process was being “abused as a vehicle to further an agenda that is at odds with…most people of this state,” even as Missouri voters had repeatedly approved measures (Medicaid expansion, cannabis legalization) that the legislature refused to enact . Ohio’s 2023 threshold campaign was explicitly about heading off policies Republican lawmakers “don’t support” – a leaked letter from the sponsor flatly said it was needed to block anticipated constitutional amendments on reproductive rights and redistricting (issues which, like cannabis, enjoyed majority public support). In Idaho, the constitutional ban on drug initiatives is a preemptive strike by prohibitionist legislators who see the writing on the wall as neighboring states embrace legalization. Florida’s officials, meanwhile, have closely guarded the gateway to constitutional amendments, knowing that despite a conservative legislature, public polling shows strong support for marijuana reform (above the 60% mark needed to pass one).

The impact of these efforts on marijuana reform is significant. In some states, voter-approved cannabis measures have been overturned or delayed – South Dakotans and Nebraskans saw their votes effectively nullified in court, and Arkansas voters never got the chance to fully enact their choice. In others, the rules have been changed to raise the bar – as in Florida’s 60% requirement, which already quashed one recreational marijuana amendment, and potentially Missouri or North Dakota’s pending changes if voters endorse them. And in states like Texas and Mississippi, voters simply have no direct say (Texas by design, Mississippi due to the court voiding its initiative process) – leaving cannabis policy entirely in the hands of legislators who, to date, have refused to move toward reform. Despite these obstacles, marijuana reform advocates continue to adapt: pursuing new petitions (sometimes with narrower language to survive legal scrutiny), launching court fights of their own, or targeting alternative pathways (such as legislative lobbying or local-level changes where possible). The tension between popular opinion and institutional roadblocks remains high. As one analysis observed, public support for cannabis legalization keeps growing, “yet institutional and political barriers remain strong”, meaning the future of reform will hinge not just on public opinion but on “sustained civic engagement, legal clarity, and the availability of democratic tools” for voters to shape policy .

Sources: Official state legislative records, state and federal court rulings, and reporting from reputable news outlets were used in compiling this report. Key examples and details are drawn from sources such as the Rockefeller Institute of Government , the Brennan Center for Justice , the Associated Press/NPR , Marijuana Moment , and state-focused news organizations (e.g. Missouri Independent ). These illustrate the breadth of strategies – from raising voting thresholds to court challenges – employed across various states to constrain voter-driven marijuana law reforms in 2023–2025.
